title: NULL handling
summary_md: Three-valued logic, the NULL-aware functions in MySQL and SQL Server, and the traps interviewers probe: NOT IN, aggregates, ordering, concatenation.

sections.heading: Three-valued logic: NULL means unknown
sections.body_md:
A comparison with NULL is neither true nor false - it is **UNKNOWN**. `WHERE` and `JOIN ... ON` keep a row only when the condition is TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows vanish.
- `NULL = NULL`, `NULL <> NULL`, `x = NULL`, `x <> NULL` are all UNKNOWN. Never write `= NULL`.
- Test with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` - the only comparisons that return TRUE/FALSE for NULL.
- `TRUE OR UNKNOWN` = TRUE, `FALSE AND UNKNOWN` = FALSE, `NOT UNKNOWN` = UNKNOWN; everything else with UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN.
- `salary <> 150000` silently drops rows whose salary is NULL - add `OR salary IS NULL` if you want them.
- `CASE col WHEN NULL THEN ...` never matches (it compiles to `col = NULL`); use `CASE WHEN col IS NULL`.
- GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION and ORDER BY treat all NULLs as one group / equal - only `=` does not.

args.name: expr
args.meaning: Any column or expression. Returns TRUE/FALSE, never UNKNOWN.

examples.title: NULL = NULL is unknown
examples.explain_md:
A CASE maps TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to labels. `NULL = NULL` falls through to unknown; `IS NULL` is TRUE.
`TRUE OR NULL` is TRUE but `TRUE AND NULL` stays unknown.
examples.mysql:
SELECT CASE WHEN NULL = NULL THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (NULL = NULL) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS null_eq_null,
       CASE WHEN NULL IS NULL THEN 'true' ELSE 'false' END AS is_null,
       CASE WHEN (1 = 1 OR NULL = 1) THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (1 = 1 OR NULL = 1) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS true_or_null,
       CASE WHEN (1 = 1 AND NULL = 1) THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (1 = 1 AND NULL = 1) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS true_and_null;
examples.tsql:
SELECT CASE WHEN NULL = NULL THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (NULL = NULL) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS null_eq_null,
       CASE WHEN NULL IS NULL THEN 'true' ELSE 'false' END AS is_null,
       CASE WHEN (1 = 1 OR NULL = 1) THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (1 = 1 OR NULL = 1) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS true_or_null,
       CASE WHEN (1 = 1 AND NULL = 1) THEN 'true' WHEN NOT (1 = 1 AND NULL = 1) THEN 'false' ELSE 'unknown' END AS true_and_null;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server has no boolean type, so a comparison cannot be selected directly - wrap it in CASE as above. (MySQL can run `SELECT NULL = NULL` and returns NULL.) With `SET ANSI_NULLS OFF` SQL Server would treat `= NULL` like `IS NULL`; that setting is deprecated, assume ON.

examples.title: = NULL finds nothing; IS NULL finds the contractor
examples.explain_md: Jon is the only employee with NULL salary. `= NULL` returns 0 rows. `<> 150000` returns 7 rows - Jon is missing - and `OR salary IS NULL` brings him back.
examples.mysql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary = NULL)            AS eq_null,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary IS NULL)           AS is_null,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary <> 150000)         AS not_150k,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary <> 150000 OR salary IS NULL) AS not_150k_or_null;
examples.tsql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary = NULL)            AS eq_null,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary IS NULL)           AS is_null,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary <> 150000)         AS not_150k,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary <> 150000 OR salary IS NULL) AS not_150k_or_null;

pitfalls_md: `WHERE col NOT IN (...)` and `col <> x` both exclude NULL rows - the most common silent data loss.
A LEFT JOIN followed by `WHERE right_table.col = 'x'` discards the NULL-extended rows and turns the join into an inner join; put that filter in ON.

sections.heading: COALESCE vs IFNULL vs ISNULL
sections.body_md:
All three replace NULL with a fallback. Prefer **COALESCE** - it is ANSI, works in both engines, and takes any number of arguments.
- `COALESCE(a, b, c, ...)` returns the first non-NULL argument, left to right; NULL if all are NULL.
- MySQL `IFNULL(a, b)`: exactly 2 arguments. **Do not** use MySQL `ISNULL(x)` as a fallback - there it is a one-argument test returning 1/0.
- SQL Server `ISNULL(a, b)`: exactly 2 arguments, but the result takes the **data type of the first argument** - the fallback is silently truncated/converted to it. COALESCE instead uses the highest-precedence type among all arguments.
- Rule of thumb: COALESCE everywhere; reach for ISNULL/IFNULL only for brevity on two args.
- Typical uses: display defaults, `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)`, first available value across columns (`COALESCE(mobile, work, home)`).

args.name: expr1, expr2, ...
args.meaning: COALESCE: checked left to right; the first one that is not NULL is returned.

args.name: IFNULL / ISNULL position 2
args.meaning: Returned when position 1 is NULL. In SQL Server it is converted to position 1's type.

examples.title: First non-NULL wins
examples.explain_md: The first non-NULL argument is returned; argument order is priority order.
examples.mysql: SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'c', 'd') AS first_non_null, COALESCE(NULL, 0) AS zero_fallback, IFNULL(NULL, 'fallback') AS two_arg_result;
examples.tsql: SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'c', 'd') AS first_non_null, COALESCE(NULL, 0) AS zero_fallback, ISNULL(NULL, 'fallback') AS two_arg_result;

examples.title: Fill missing salary
examples.explain_md: Jon (NULL salary) becomes 0 / -1. Put COALESCE in the SELECT list; in a WHERE it blocks index use.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, COALESCE(salary, 0) AS salary_or_zero, IFNULL(salary, -1) AS salary_or_minus1 FROM employees WHERE emp_id >= 8 ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, COALESCE(salary, 0) AS salary_or_zero, ISNULL(salary, -1) AS salary_or_minus1 FROM employees WHERE emp_id >= 8 ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: ISNULL takes the first argument's type
examples.explain_md: The first argument is declared as a 3-character string. In SQL Server `ISNULL` forces the fallback into that type, so `'abcdef'` becomes `'abc'`; `COALESCE` keeps `'abcdef'`. MySQL `IFNULL` has no such problem.
examples.mysql: SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 'abcdef') AS coalesce_result, IFNULL(NULL, 'abcdef') AS two_arg_result;
examples.tsql: SELECT COALESCE(CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR(3)), 'abcdef') AS coalesce_result, ISNULL(CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR(3)), 'abcdef') AS two_arg_result;
examples.dialect_note_md: Real SQL Server returns `abcdef` and `abc` (ISNULL truncates to VARCHAR(3)); MySQL returns `abcdef` for both. The same effect bites with INT vs DECIMAL: `ISNULL(int_col, 1.5)` returns an INT.

pitfalls_md: SQL Server `COALESCE(NULL, NULL)` errors (at least one argument must have a type); cast one to a type.
`WHERE COALESCE(col, 0) = 0` cannot use an index on `col` in either engine; write `col = 0 OR col IS NULL` instead.

sections.heading: NULLIF: turn a value into NULL (divide-by-zero guard)
sections.body_md:
`NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when `a = b`, otherwise `a`. It is the inverse of COALESCE.
- Divide-by-zero guard: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` yields NULL instead of an error.
- SQL Server **raises an error** on `/ 0`. MySQL returns NULL for `SELECT 1/0` but **errors on INSERT/UPDATE** in strict mode - guard anyway.
- Clean sentinels: `NULLIF(TRIM(col), '')` turns empty strings into real NULLs; `NULLIF(col, 'N/A')`.
- Pair them: `COALESCE(x / NULLIF(y, 0), 0)` for "ratio, or 0 when undefined".

args.name: expr1
args.meaning: Returned unchanged unless it equals expr2.

args.name: expr2
args.meaning: The 'bad' value; when expr1 = expr2 the result is NULL.

examples.title: Safe ratio with NULLIF
examples.explain_md: The row with x = 0 would divide by zero; `NULLIF(x, 0)` makes the denominator NULL so the ratio is NULL, and COALESCE turns it into 0 for display.

examples.title: NULLIF on a sentinel value
examples.explain_md: `NULLIF(manager_id, 1)` hides everyone managed by Ana (id 1) behind NULL - a quick way to make an aggregate skip a value. `COUNT(NULLIF(...))` counts only the other rows.
examples.mysql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(manager_id) AS has_manager, COUNT(NULLIF(manager_id, 1)) AS manager_not_ana FROM employees;
examples.tsql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(manager_id) AS has_manager, COUNT(NULLIF(manager_id, 1)) AS manager_not_ana FROM employees;

sections.heading: NULLs in aggregates
sections.body_md:
Aggregates skip NULL inputs - which changes averages and counts.
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values.
- `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` ignore NULLs. `AVG(col)` = `SUM(col) / COUNT(col)`, **not** `/ COUNT(*)`.
- To average NULL as zero: `AVG(COALESCE(col, 0))`.
- An aggregate over zero rows, or only NULLs, returns NULL (except COUNT, which returns 0): use `COALESCE(SUM(col), 0)`.
- SQL Server `AVG` of an INT column returns an INT (truncated): use `AVG(col * 1.0)`.
- GROUP BY puts all NULLs in one group.

examples.title: AVG skips Jon's NULL salary
examples.explain_md: 9 of 10 employees have a salary. `AVG(salary)` divides by 9; `AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0))` divides by 10. `SUM` over an empty set is NULL, hence the COALESCE.
examples.mysql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(salary) AS salary_n,
       AVG(salary * 1.0) AS avg_ignoring_null,
       AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0) * 1.0) AS avg_null_as_zero,
       COALESCE((SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Nowhere'), 0) AS sum_of_nothing
FROM employees;
examples.tsql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(salary) AS salary_n,
       AVG(salary * 1.0) AS avg_ignoring_null,
       AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0) * 1.0) AS avg_null_as_zero,
       COALESCE((SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Nowhere'), 0) AS sum_of_nothing
FROM employees;

examples.title: NULL is its own group
examples.explain_md: `city` is NULL for Olga; GROUP BY returns one NULL row (sorted first in both engines) whose `COUNT(city)` is 0 while `COUNT(*)` is 1.
examples.mysql: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS city_values FROM customers GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;
examples.tsql: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS city_values FROM customers GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;

pitfalls_md: `COUNT(col) = COUNT(*)` is a quick 'column has no NULLs' check.
`SUM(a) - SUM(b)` is not `SUM(a - b)` when either column has NULLs: rows with a NULL in one column are dropped from the second form only.

sections.heading: NOT IN with NULL: the classic trap
sections.body_md:
`x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` expands to `x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL` - the last term is UNKNOWN, so the whole predicate is never TRUE. **One NULL in the subquery empties the result.**
- Fix 1: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.k = outer.k)` - NULL-safe, and the usual anti-join.
- Fix 2: filter the subquery: `NOT IN (SELECT k FROM t WHERE k IS NOT NULL)`.
- Fix 3: `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.k IS NULL` (join on a non-NULL key).
- `IN` is harmless: a NULL in the list just never matches.
- Hits "employees who manage nobody" and "customers with no orders" whenever the child key can be NULL.

examples.title: NOT IN returns zero rows
examples.explain_md: `manager_id` contains Ana's NULL, so `emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id ...)` is never TRUE: **no rows**, even though five employees manage nobody.
examples.mysql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: NOT EXISTS gives the right answer
examples.explain_md: Employees who are nobody's manager: Dev, Eli, Gus, Hal, Jon.
examples.mysql: SELECT e.emp_id, e.name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees m WHERE m.manager_id = e.emp_id) ORDER BY e.emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT e.emp_id, e.name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees m WHERE m.manager_id = e.emp_id) ORDER BY e.emp_id;

examples.title: NOT IN works if the subquery excludes NULLs
examples.explain_md: Same rows as NOT EXISTS once `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` removes the NULL from the list.
examples.mysql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY emp_id;

pitfalls_md: The trap only fires when the **subquery/list can contain NULL**. A NOT NULL column makes NOT IN safe - until the schema changes. Default to NOT EXISTS in interviews.
`NULL NOT IN (1, 2)` (NULL on the left) is also UNKNOWN: the row is dropped.

sections.heading: NULL ordering and emulating NULLS LAST
sections.body_md:
Both MySQL and SQL Server treat NULL as the **lowest** value: first in `ASC`, last in `DESC`. Neither supports `NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST` (PostgreSQL and Oracle do, and sort NULLs high by default).
- Portable NULLS LAST for ASC: `ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, col`.
- MySQL shortcut: `ORDER BY col IS NULL, col` (a boolean sorts 0 < 1). SQL Server cannot sort a boolean - use the CASE form.
- NULLS FIRST for DESC: `ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, col DESC`.
- The same trick works inside window `ORDER BY`.
- `MAX/MIN` ignore NULLs, so `MIN(col)` is the smallest non-NULL value even though NULL sorts lowest.

syntax.mysql:
ORDER BY col IS NULL, col   -- NULLS LAST (ASC)
ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, col   -- portable
syntax.tsql: ORDER BY CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, col

examples.title: Default: NULL sorts first ascending
examples.explain_md: Jon (NULL salary) is on top for `ASC`.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY salary, emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY salary, emp_id;

examples.title: NULLS LAST with a CASE sort key
examples.explain_md: The first sort key is 0 for real values and 1 for NULL, so Jon drops to the bottom while salaries stay ascending.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, salary, emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, salary, emp_id;

examples.title: DESC with NULLs first
examples.explain_md: Highest salary first but the NULL pinned on top (default DESC would put it last).
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, salary DESC, emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept IN ('Marketing', 'Sales') ORDER BY CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, salary DESC, emp_id;

sections.heading: NULL-safe equality
sections.body_md:
Sometimes two NULLs should count as 'the same' (diffing snapshots, SCD change detection, joining on nullable keys).
- MySQL: `a <=> b` is TRUE if both equal or both NULL, never UNKNOWN. `NOT (a <=> b)` finds changes.
- SQL Server 2022+: `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` / `a IS DISTINCT FROM b`. Not in older versions, and MySQL does not support it.
- Portable (any version): `a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL)`.
- `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT` / `UNION` / `DISTINCT` already treat NULLs as equal in both engines - a neat shortcut for row diffs.

syntax.tsql: a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b   -- 2022+

args.name: b
args.meaning: Right operand; may be NULL. TRUE when a = b or both are NULL.

examples.title: Literal truth table
examples.explain_md: MySQL `<=>` returns 1/0; the SQL Server 2022 operator is wrapped in CASE because a predicate cannot be selected directly.
examples.mysql: SELECT NULL <=> NULL AS both_null, 1 <=> NULL AS one_null, 1 <=> 1 AS equal;
examples.tsql: SELECT CASE WHEN NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS both_null, CASE WHEN 1 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS one_null, CASE WHEN 1 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS equal;
examples.dialect_note_md: `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` needs SQL Server 2022 (compatibility level 160). On 2019 and older use `(a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL))`.

examples.title: Find changed prices between two snapshots
examples.explain_md: Items 3 and 4 changed (30 to NULL, NULL to 45); items 1 and 2 are unchanged. Item 2 is NULL in both snapshots: plain `<>` would miss real changes involving NULL, and plain `=` would wrongly flag item 2.

tables.name: price_old
tables.description_md: Yesterday's prices; items 2 and 4 have no price.

examples.mysql: SELECT o.item_id, o.price AS old_price, n.price AS new_price FROM price_old o JOIN price_new n ON n.item_id = o.item_id WHERE NOT (o.price <=> n.price) ORDER BY o.item_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT o.item_id, o.price AS old_price, n.price AS new_price FROM price_old o JOIN price_new n ON n.item_id = o.item_id WHERE NOT (o.price = n.price OR (o.price IS NULL AND n.price IS NULL)) ORDER BY o.item_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: On SQL Server 2022 the filter can be `WHERE o.price IS DISTINCT FROM n.price`. The portable form above works on every version.

sections.heading: CONCAT and NULL
sections.body_md:
The engines disagree - a favourite gotcha.
- MySQL `CONCAT(a, b, ...)` returns **NULL if any argument is NULL**. `CONCAT_WS(sep, a, b, ...)` **skips NULL** arguments (and never emits a dangling separator).
- SQL Server `CONCAT(...)` treats NULL as an **empty string** (2012+). `CONCAT_WS` (2017+) also skips NULLs.
- SQL Server `a + b` follows the NULL rule: result is NULL if either side is NULL (default `CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL ON`).
- MySQL has no `+` for strings (it adds numbers: `'a' + 'b'` = 0) and `||` is logical OR by default.
- Portable: `CONCAT(a, ' ', COALESCE(b, ''))`.

syntax.tsql:
CONCAT(s1, s2 [, ...])
CONCAT_WS(separator, s1, s2 [, ...])  -- 2017+
s1 + s2

args.name: separator (CONCAT_WS position 1)
args.meaning: Text inserted between non-NULL values. A NULL separator makes the result NULL.

args.name: s1, s2, ...
args.meaning: Values to join; numbers are converted to text.

examples.title: Literal comparison
examples.explain_md: MySQL `CONCAT` is NULL as soon as one piece is NULL; `CONCAT_WS` skips it; COALESCE patches it.
examples.mysql: SELECT CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b') AS concat_null, CONCAT_WS('-', 'a', NULL, 'b') AS concat_ws_skips, CONCAT('a', COALESCE(NULL, ''), 'b') AS coalesce_fix;
examples.tsql: SELECT 'a' + NULL + 'b' AS concat_null, CONCAT_WS('-', 'a', NULL, 'b') AS concat_ws_skips, CONCAT('a', COALESCE(NULL, ''), 'b') AS coalesce_fix;
examples.dialect_note_md: The T-SQL above uses `+` to show the NULL result. SQL Server's own `CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b')` returns `ab`, not NULL - the opposite of MySQL.

examples.title: Name and city
examples.explain_md: Olga has no city. The naive join is NULL; `CONCAT_WS` and `COALESCE` give usable text.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, CONCAT(name, ', ', city) AS naive, CONCAT_WS(', ', name, city) AS skipped, CONCAT(name, ' (', COALESCE(city, 'n/a'), ')') AS labelled FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (1, 3) ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, name + ', ' + city AS naive, CONCAT_WS(', ', name, city) AS skipped, CONCAT(name, ' (', COALESCE(city, 'n/a'), ')') AS labelled FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (1, 3) ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: `naive` is NULL for Olga in MySQL via `CONCAT` and in SQL Server via `+`. SQL Server's `CONCAT(name, ', ', city)` would instead return `Olga Petrova, ` (NULL as empty).
